subject: ent
title: Orbital Complications: Chandler Classification and Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis

steps.tx: **Chandler classification** stages orbital complications of sinusitis in five ascending groups, from preseptal inflammation through orbital cellulitis and abscess to cavernous sinus thrombosis. Ethmoid sinusitis in children is the usual source, spreading through the paper thin lamina papyracea or valveless veins into the orbit. The staging matters because management escalates from antibiotics alone to urgent surgical drainage across the groups.
steps.say: Five ascending stages organise how sinus infection invades the orbit in children and adults. Ethmoid infection crosses the paper thin orbital wall or valveless veins to reach orbital tissues. Higher stages demand surgery, so accurate staging drives the whole management plan.

vis.alt: Coronal illustration showing ostiomeatal obstruction, mucosal oedema and purulent exudate in the maxillary sinus adjacent to the orbit.
vis.caption: Sinus infection beside the thin orbital wall that orbital complications cross. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Group one is **periorbital oedema** from venous congestion without true orbital infection, showing lid swelling with normal eye movements, vision and globe position. Group two, orbital cellulitis, infiltrates orbital fat diffusely and brings painful restricted movements and chemosis without a discrete collection. Both early groups often respond to intravenous antibiotics with close ophthalmic observation, provided vision and movements are checked repeatedly.
steps.say: Lid swelling with a normal quiet eye marks the earliest congestive stage needing only antibiotics. Diffuse infiltration next brings painful restricted movements without any discrete pus collection forming. Repeated vision and movement checks guard both stages against silent progression.

steps.tx: Group three, **subperiosteal abscess**, collects pus between the lamina papyracea and orbital periosteum, displacing the globe downward and outward from an ethmoid source. Group four, orbital abscess, collects pus within orbital fat itself with severe proptosis, complete ophthalmoplegia and threatened vision. Both abscess groups generally need surgical drainage of abscess and source sinus together, with small medial collections in young children as the debated exception.
steps.say: Pus between bone and periosteum pushes the globe away from the infected ethmoid sinus. Collections inside orbital fat itself cause severe protrusion with complete movement loss and threatened sight. Drainage of abscess plus source sinus treats both advanced abscess groups.

vis.title: Chandler groups three to five
rows: Critical care, image brain and veins

steps.tx: This scan shows a **subperiosteal abscess**, pus gathered between the paper-thin lamina papyracea and the orbital periosteum beside it. Ethmoid infection crosses that fragile wall or its veins, then lifts the periosteum into a lens-shaped collection. The globe is pushed downward and outward, away from the sinus. Size, vision changes and failure to improve decide between antibiotics alone and drainage.
steps.say: Pus between bone and periosteum pushes the globe away from the infected ethmoid sinus. Drainage of the abscess protects vision when collections enlarge or sight begins to fail.

vis.alt: CT of the orbit showing a lens-shaped subperiosteal collection along the medial orbital wall pushing the globe downward and outward away from the ethmoid sinus.
vis.caption: Pus lifting the periosteum off the lamina papyracea displaces the eye away from the infected ethmoid, the hallmark of Chandler group three. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Orbital cellulitis** must be separated from preseptal cellulitis at the bedside, because only orbital disease threatens sight and intracranial spread. Pain on eye movement, restricted movements, proptosis, chemosis, reduced vision or colour desaturation and a relative afferent pupillary defect each mark postseptal involvement. Any one of these signs converts lid swelling into an emergency needing contrast imaging and joint specialty care.
steps.say: Painful movements, protrusion or any vision change separates dangerous orbital infection from surface cellulitis. Colour desaturation and pupillary defects warn that the optic nerve is suffering already. Such signs convert simple lid swelling into an imaging and referral emergency.

steps.tx: Contrast enhanced computed tomography of sinuses and orbits is the first imaging test, showing the source sinus, lamina dehiscence, subperiosteal collections and globe displacement in minutes. Magnetic resonance follows when intracranial extension, cavernous sinus disease or optic nerve compromise is suspected, or when radiation avoidance matters in children needing repeat scans. **Vision charting** with acuity, colour plates and pupil checks runs alongside imaging, never after it.
steps.say: Contrast scanning of sinuses and orbits quickly reveals source, wall defects and pus collections. Magnetic resonance follows whenever brain, venous sinus or optic nerve involvement is suspected clinically. Vision, colour and pupil charting proceeds alongside imaging rather than waiting afterwards.

steps.tx: **Frontal mucocele** is an expansile mucus filled cyst of an obstructed frontal or ethmoid sinus that remodels bone slowly over years, displacing the globe downward and outward with a painless forehead or orbital swelling. Old trauma or surgery often precedes it by a decade or more. Treatment marsupialises the mucocele widely into the nose endoscopically so it drains permanently instead of reforming behind a narrow opening.
steps.say: Slowly expanding mucus cysts from blocked sinuses displace the eye painlessly over years. Old trauma or surgery is present a decade or longer before presentation in many cases. Wide endoscopic marsupialisation into the nose drains the cyst permanently and prevents reformation.

vis.alt: Coronal and sagittal diagrams of nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses showing the frontal and ethmoid sinuses from which mucoceles expand.
vis.caption: Frontal and ethmoid sinuses, the usual origin of orbital mucoceles. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Cavernous sinus thrombosis**, Chandler group five, spreads infected clot through valveless veins to the cavernous sinus, producing high fever, bilateral periorbital oedema, chemosis, proptosis and palsies of the third, fourth, fifth and sixth cranial nerves. Bilateral eye signs distinguish it from unilateral orbital abscess and signal grave prognosis without rapid treatment. Sphenoid sinusitis is a classic source alongside midface skin infection.
steps.say: Infected clot reaching the cavernous sinus produces fever with swelling of both eyes together. Multiple cranial nerve palsies with protrusion and congestion indicate this gravest stage. Bilateral involvement separates venous sinus thrombosis from a one sided orbital abscess.

vis.alt: MRI and MR venography showing cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with sulcal hyperintensity on axial FLAIR imaging.
vis.caption: Venous sinus thrombosis on MRI and venography. Image: Wolf et al., CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

steps.tx: Management of cavernous sinus thrombosis combines high dose intravenous antibiotics, drainage of the source sinus, critical care support and urgent neuroimaging, with anticoagulation debated case by case. Source control in the sphenoid or ethmoid sinus should not be delayed while debating adjuncts. **Mortality** remains substantial even with modern care, and survivors may keep visual loss or nerve palsies, so prevention through early orbital staging is worth more than late rescue.
steps.say: High dose intravenous antibiotics plus source sinus drainage anchor treatment of venous sinus thrombosis. Anticoagulation remains debated individually while critical care support continues alongside antibiotics. Outcomes stay grave despite modern care, rewarding early staging over late rescue.

steps.tx: Children deserve a lower imaging threshold than adults because they localise orbital signs poorly and deteriorate faster from ethmoid disease. A medial subperiosteal abscess in a young child with good vision may trial antibiotics under hourly observation in some centres. **Deterioration triggers** including visual change, enlarging proptosis or failure to improve within a day mandate drainage without further delay regardless of initial plans.
steps.say: Young children deteriorate faster and localise eye signs poorly, which lowers the imaging threshold considerably. Small medial collections with good vision sometimes need only antibiotics under hourly observation protocols. Any visual change or failure to improve within a day requires drainage.

nodes.label: Vision, colour, pupil and movement checks
Contrast CT if any orbital sign

steps.tx: Examination memory for this cluster is direct. Five Chandler groups ascend from oedema to venous thrombosis, subperiosteal pus displaces the globe away from its source, and bilateral signs mean cavernous sinus disease. A painless globe displaced downward and outward years after trauma suggests mucocele rather than infection. **Hourly eye observations** are treatment, not paperwork, whenever orbital infection is managed without immediate surgery.
steps.say: Five stages ascending from lid oedema to venous thrombosis organise every examination answer here. Pus under periosteum gives globe displacement away from its ethmoid source in a characteristic direction. Hourly eye observations are active treatment whenever surgery is initially withheld.

cards.b: One preseptal oedema, two orbital cellulitis, three subperiosteal abscess, four orbital abscess, five cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Orbital: painful restricted movements, proptosis, chemosis, vision or colour loss, pupillary defect. Preseptal: lid signs only.
Painless globe displacement downward and outward years after trauma or surgery; treat by wide endoscopic marsupialisation.

keys: Ethmoid sinusitis in children is the usual orbital source
Bilateral eye signs mean cavernous sinus thrombosis
Any vision change in orbital infection is an emergency
